h: The Rejinagar bypoll: police on the road to the booth, voters sent back
dek: On bypoll day in Muslim-majority Rejinagar in Bengal, people in several villages said they were stopped from voting, and local journalists' pages were shut down before polling.
body: On Tuesday 6 October, a bypoll was held for the Rejinagar seat in West Bengal. Scroll's reporters went from village to village all day, and what they saw did not match the Election Commission's claim of a 'peaceful and fair' poll. At a school booth in Nazirpur the queue was moving in the morning, but men walking towards the booth were being forcibly sent back while the police and paramilitary forces stood and watched.

About twelve kilometres away, in Maradighi village, there were more than two and a half thousand voters across four booths. More than a dozen people said the booths had already been captured. The police told one young man that his vote had already been cast. Many people did not leave home at all, out of fear of violence.

Muslims make up sixty to seventy percent of Rejinagar's population. The opposition says the BJP cannot win such a seat without the government machinery. Humayun Kabir had won from here and from Nowda and kept Nowda, which is why this bypoll was held. His party fielded his son. Kabir claims that 64 of his workers were sent to jail before the vote, and that he himself was detained on the morning of polling. People working for the CPI(M) and Trinamool candidates also said their polling agents were picked up at night, or had their papers taken and were sent home.

In the week before the election, the social media pages of several local journalists in Murshidabad were blocked, among them a page with seven and a half lakh (750,000) followers. Most pages came back only after voting ended. One journalist said this also wiped out his advertising income.
The same day there was also a bypoll in Nandigram, where one candidate withdrew after meeting Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, and the Congress candidate was arrested in old cases.
nazar: The right to vote is the most basic right of a citizen, and the people turned back from the booths here were mostly Muslims. When men in uniform stand and watch and the voices of local journalists are silenced, it is no longer about one seat. It becomes a question of trust in the whole democracy.

It is also worth remembering that Trinamool's own people admit there was rigging under their rule too. Those in power change; the method stays the same. The Commission should openly investigate every allegation, because silence is also an answer.
sawal: If your vote has 'already been cast', where do you complain?
ref: Rejinagar
An Assembly seat in West Bengal's Murshidabad district, where Muslims are in the majority. Humayun Kabir won from here in the 2026 Assembly election.
Election observers
Officers sent by the Election Commission to watch over polling and hear complaints of wrongdoing. There are both general and police observers.
ank: workers sent to jail before the vote, Kabir claims
followers on a local news page that was blocked

h: Three years of Gaza: much destruction, no victory anywhere
dek: Refaat Ibrahim argues that Israel has laid Gaza waste but has not achieved even one of its declared goals.
body: Three years after the attack of October 2023, Gaza writer Refaat Ibrahim asks a simple question: can a body count be called victory? According to him, more than 74,000 people have been killed and more than 180,000 injured, hunger has spread, and hospitals, schools, water and electricity have been destroyed. Even so, the real measure of a war is the terms on which it ends.

The writer tests Israel's four declared goals one by one. On the hostages, the army managed to free only eight of 250 alive; most were released through negotiations with Hamas. The claim of destroying Hamas is also incomplete. It still controls parts of Gaza, and Israel has to bargain to get it to lay down its weapons.

The army sits on about 60 percent of Gaza, but it finds the cost of fully occupying the rest too high. The 'Board of Peace' and new administrative structure, set up by sidelining the United Nations, never took shape on the ground. The attempt to push people out through hunger and by destroying their homes also failed. Most Palestinians have stayed, and some have even come back from Egypt.

In the writer's view, Israel's biggest defeat is its reputation. Last month, during Netanyahu's speech at the UN General Assembly, delegates of most countries got up and walked out, and there is an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against him. In Pew's survey of 36 countries, 67 percent of people had a negative view of Israel, and 60 percent even in the United States.
His conclusion is that force can impose conditions for a while, but it cannot create political legitimacy. A cause that has lived in people's hearts for decades cannot be wiped out with bombs.
nazar: Even after three years, the debate on Gaza often gets stuck in figures of military success. This article reminds us that peace does not come from the power of one side, but from justice and a political solution.

For a country like India, which claims to be the voice of the Global South, this is not a time just for balancing. It is a time to speak clearly for a ceasefire, for relief and for the rights of Palestinians.
sawal: If force cannot bring victory, what is the bombing for?
ref: Board of Peace
An arrangement set up at the initiative of the United States for administration and rebuilding in Gaza after the war, in which the United Nations was given no role.
International Criminal Court
A court based in The Hague that tries people accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

h: Form 6: the court did not approve it, the Commission kept saying it did
dek: The Supreme Court said clearly that it had not approved the changed Form 6, yet the Election Commission keeps repeating the opposite claim in its 'fact-check'.
body: On 5 October the Supreme Court refused to suspend Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on an interim basis, but during the hearing Chief Justice Surya Kant said something important: the court has not approved any changed Form 6. Form 6 is the application through which a new voter gets their name added to the electoral roll. In response, the Commission posted a 'fact-check' on X and repeated what it had said in its 26 September press note, that the court had upheld this declaration form. The Wire says this claim is misleading.

In June 2025, for Bihar's Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the Commission added a declaration that asked for one of eleven documents. In October 2025, in the second phase, a second page was added, in which parents' details had to be matched with the previous SIR list. In May 2026 the Supreme Court upheld the Bihar declaration, but also warned that this power of the Commission is not unlimited and must stay within the law.

Then in July 2026 the online Form 6 was changed so that the application does not move forward at all without the parents' old details. This change was never considered in the court's May judgment. Under the law, to change Form 6 the government has to amend the 1960 rules, which Parliament keeps an eye on.

According to reports in the Indian Express, two election commissioners themselves, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, wrote in May that the form could not be changed without changing the rules, and in August Sandhu called the change illegal and asked for it to be removed at once. The question is: in a three-member Commission, on whose say was this change made despite two members disagreeing?
The Wire sent the Commission a long list of questions, which had not been answered by the time of publication.
nazar: One page of one form seems a small thing, but for the poor, for migrants and for young people voting for the first time, finding a grandparent's or parent's entry in an old list is not easy. Those who cannot gather the documents quietly get left off the list.
If a constitutional body presents the court's own words upside down and ignores the objections of its own commissioners, the damage to its credibility is bigger than any one election.
sawal: If two commissioners were against it, who changed the form?
ref: Form 6

The application to add a new name to the electoral roll, set out under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The power to change it lies with the central government, after consulting the Commission.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision, in which the electoral roll is made afresh and every voter is asked for documents. It started in Bihar and is now under way in several states.

h: Khargone's cotton: the farmer's crop, someone else's price
dek: Cotton farmers in Madhya Pradesh begin picking in October, but whether the mandi is shut or prices fall, the loss lands on them every time.
body: Khargone is among the biggest cotton-growing districts of Madhya Pradesh. Cotton is sown here on about 2.25 lakh (225,000) hectares. Sowing happens in May and picking runs from October to December. In these months, cotton worth crores of rupees is sold every day in the district's mandi (wholesale farm market).

In October 2022, just as the crop was about to reach the mandi, traders went on strike demanding a cut in mandi tax. All the mandis stayed shut for eight days. Before the strike the price in Khargone was Rs 8,740 a quintal; when the mandi opened, it had fallen by about Rs 900. The government's minimum support price that year was Rs 6,380.

Sandeep Yadav of Gogaon tehsil grows cotton on ten acres. He borrowed money to pay the pickers' wages, refused to sell at the fallen price and kept the crop at home. The year before, pests had eaten more than half his crop, and before that the mandis were shut during the pandemic. He has a debt of about Rs 15 lakh, including money from a moneylender. In January he finally had to sell, for household expenses and a family wedding, and when he did the sums, nothing was left in his hands.

According to Sandeep, seeds, fertiliser, labour and pesticide together cost about Rs 15,000 an acre. Twenty-year-old Sanjay Yadav of Barwah believes the price should be at least ten thousand. Radheshyam Patel of Sabda village says that to sow the next crop too they have to borrow money on interest, and if the crop fails, the farmer drowns in debt.

Farmers' groups and farm experts both say the same thing: the support price should go up, and buying below it should be legally barred. The basic point of the report is that the farmer carries the whole burden of cost, weather, pests and the market, but has no say in setting the price.
nazar: Right now cotton picking is starting in Malwa, Vidarbha and Telangana, and farmers face the same question again: who will set the price? As long as the support price stays a paper announcement with no guarantee in the mandi, the small farmer will keep getting crushed between the trader and the moneylender.
sawal: Why does the one who grows the crop get no share in its price?
ref: Minimum support price (MSP)
The central government announces this minimum price for some crops every year. But for most crops there is no legal guarantee of purchase at this price.
Mandi tax
A fee on every purchase in an agricultural produce market, set by state governments. Madhya Pradesh's was counted among the highest in the country.

h: Adivasi students walked hundreds of kilometres; the answer was police buses
dek: Adivasi students who came from Nashik to Mumbai to protest deaths and neglect in ashram schools were detained two days in a row and sent out of the city.
body: Adivasi (indigenous) students from Maharashtra set out on foot from Nashik on 28 September. Their complaint is about deaths, unsafe conditions and the lack of basic facilities in government ashram schools and hostels. When they reached Mumbai they were not allowed to sit in protest at Azad Maidan, so they stayed at Tilak Bhavan, the Congress office.

On 5 October the police took them out of Tilak Bhavan towards Kopri in Thane, made them change vehicles several times and stopped them at many places. The Congress alleges the students were threatened and detained at three in the night. The next day they were not allowed to leave the office at all, and were put on private buses and sent off towards Jalgaon, Nandurbar and Nashik. Videos that came out show the police pushing protesters towards the buses, among them a woman holding a child.

The students' demands are clear: an independent inquiry into the deaths in ashram schools; compensation of one crore rupees each to the families of three girls who allegedly died of snakebite at Japtalai in Gadchiroli, and fifty lakh to the injured; an inquiry into irregularities in the distribution of grants; the resignation of Tribal Development Minister Ashok Uike; and better scholarships, food, sanitation and hostels.

Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis says the demands have been accepted and that the agitation is being run by some NSUI office-bearers. The police have denied making arrests from Tilak Bhavan. The Congress called it a strangling of the right to protest and also alleged that women students were mistreated.

The students do not accept that the matter is over. They have announced they will return to Azad Maidan on 25 October. The report concludes that there is a deep gap between the government's claims and the students' experience.
nazar: Ashram schools are the only path to education for Adivasi children. If children die there of snakebite, and then their fellow students who come to ask for justice are packed into buses and pushed out of the capital, it is not just a failure of administration. It is a question of what an Adivasi life is worth.
If the demands really have been accepted, it is the government's duty to put them in writing with a timeline, not to use sticks and buses.
sawal: Since when has asking about children's deaths become a crime?
ref: Ashram school
Residential schools in Maharashtra for Adivasi children, run or aided by the government, where living, food and schooling come together.
Azad Maidan
An open ground in south Mumbai that for decades has been a well-known site for protests by workers, farmers and students.

h: Bengal's Christians go to the human rights commission, with a record of attacks
dek: A West Bengal Christian forum has gone to three commissions with complaints of attacks on house churches and prayer meetings, edited videos and police laxity.
body: On 5 October, Bangiya Christiya Pariseva, a joint forum of different Christian denominations in West Bengal, filed complaints with the National Human Rights Commission, the State Human Rights Commission and the National Commission for Minorities. It alleges that over the past three months there have been targeted attacks, vandalism and desecration at small house churches and prayer meetings across the state.

The same day, a public hearing was held at Park Circus in Kolkata, where pastors, victims and eyewitnesses spoke. People from the human rights groups APDR and MASUM, and former IAS officer Jawhar Sircar, were also there. Alt News has already recorded at least 35 incidents of violence and threats between 1 July and 20 September, mostly in the interior of Bengal.

The forum has four main complaints. First, worshippers were attacked, and some well-known people played this down as public protest. Second, the attackers cut selected parts into videos and spread the charge of conversion by inducement, which also misled local officials. Third, the police let the attackers go and questioned victims late at night, and only after a heavy legal effort were FIRs filed, in just 13 cases. Fourth, officials refused even to talk to church leaders.

Citing Articles 14, 19, 21 and 25 of the Constitution, the forum has asked the commissions to order the state government and the DGP to hold a high-level independent inquiry, to investigate the online propaganda, to file FIRs at once in pending cases, and to give house churches police protection during weekly prayers.
The report rests on the forum's allegations and testimonies; it does not include a response from the Bengal police or administration.
nazar: The noise about conversion often starts with an edited video and ends in mob violence. The small house churches in Bengal's villages mostly belong to Dalit, Adivasi and poor families, so this is an attack on people at the margins as well as on a minority community.
Freedom of worship is a promise of the Constitution. If the police put the victim in the dock, that promise stays only on paper.
sawal: How many prayers can one edited video stop?
ref: House church
A small prayer meeting held in a room or courtyard of a home, common in villages and poor settlements where there is no big church.
Article 25
The provision of the Constitution that gives every person the freedom to profess, practise and propagate their religion.

h: Where do the poor stand in the plan to cope with climate change?
dek: India is drawing up its first National Adaptation Plan, and three researchers ask who its benefits will reach.
by: Ishan Kukreti, Sarada Prasanna Das, Soni R K
body: This year Assam and Bihar went under floods, while Maharashtra declared drought, and Rajasthan, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu also face drought-like conditions. The Reserve Bank has warned that extreme heat and humidity will cut working hours, and that up to four and a half percent of the country's GDP could be at stake by 2030. In this situation the government is making its first National Adaptation Plan, which will set the direction of public spending on protection for decades.

Three researchers from the Sustainable Futures Collaborative say that in the debate on cutting emissions, talk of a 'just transition' is now common, but adaptation is assumed to be good in itself. In fact it too involves choices: whose risk is counted first, where the money goes, and whose knowledge is valued. This decides who is saved and who is left behind.

Take cities. There are heat action plans and warning systems, but the burden of escaping the heat is mostly put on households: air conditioners, cool roofs, better buildings. People living in bastis (informal settlements) cannot afford these costs. The writers ask for public cool spaces, shaded streets and better housing.

In farming, solar irrigation schemes like PM-KUSUM mostly help individual farmers, which leaves out small, marginal and sharecropping farmers. Community solar irrigation could be a better way. Hills, coasts, forests and fields each face different risks, so a one-size plan will not work.

The writers welcome the plan's mention of traditional knowledge, but ask whether hill people's understanding of slopes, or fishers' reading of the coast, will really find a place in the schemes. They want consultation to be legally required, budgets to be shared out according to the most vulnerable areas, and independent monitoring of whether the benefits reached the most vulnerable.
nazar: Workers in slums, sharecroppers and fishers are the first to be hit by floods and heatwaves, but plans are often made without asking them. If adaptation money also flows where comfort already exists, the climate crisis will deepen inequality further.
Only making the consent of the gram sabha (village assembly) and the basti a condition of the plan can make it a people's plan.
sawal: In the end, whose pocket will pay the bill for protection from the heat?
ref: National Adaptation Plan (NAP)
Under the Paris Agreement, countries make long-term plans to deal with the effects of climate change. India is now preparing its first such plan.
PM-KUSUM
A central government scheme that gives farmers subsidies to set up solar pumps and small solar plants on their fields.

h: One fight across the border: the daughters of Delhi and Swat
dek: Fauzia Yazdani shows that in India and Pakistan, when women voice anger over rape, it is their language that gets questioned, less so the criminals.
body: India and Pakistan together are home to about a fifth of the world's population, and in both, women are around half. Yet their share in the workforce is about 24 percent in Pakistan and 32 percent in India, and most of that work happens inside the home, without any protection. The writer says education and jobs matter only when they turn into rights, a voice and confidence in public space.

She puts two September incidents side by side. In Delhi, after the gang rape of a 17-year-old student, women students took to the streets, and the demand went beyond safe movement to breaking patriarchy. In Swat, after the rape and murder of a nine-year-old girl, women protested for justice and police accountability.

The same pattern shows in both countries. As soon as women raise slogans in anger, the debate moves away from the crime to their clothes, their language and their conduct. Delhi University's slogans were called obscene, just as in Pakistan the Aurat March's 'My body, my choice' was called against religion and culture. The writer lists statements by leaders on both sides that blamed clothes for violence.

The writer draws a line between two views. One is about 'protection', which wants to save women by putting restrictions on them. The other is about 'citizenship', which says a woman should make her own life choices and that stopping violence is the state's job. The constitutions of both countries guarantee equality and dignity; what is missing is enforcement.

She says the reason a movement like Delhi's is not seen in Pakistan is not women's silence but the heavy price of coming out on the street: disgrace, losing schooling, fear of revenge. The real question is whether, after violence, it is women who are reined in, or whether criminals, institutions and the government are held to account.
nazar: On both sides of the border, women's pain and their fight are the same. This article shows that one road to peace in South Asia also runs through recognising shared experiences like these.

Here too, after a rape, questions are raised about the survivor's clothes and about going out at night. The equality the Constitution has given will be real only when the questions are put to the criminal and the system.
sawal: Why fear women's slogans and not men's violence?
ref: Aurat March
A march held in Pakistan's cities on International Women's Day since 2018, demanding women's rights and freedom.
Swat
A valley in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province that was once in the headlines because of Taliban control and Malala Yousafzai.

h: Journalist covering a protest alleges molestation; no FIR
dek: An independent journalist covering a protest in Delhi against the Chief Election Commissioner accused an ACP of molestation, but two days later the police had still not registered a case.
body: On 3 October a protest was going on in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Near Kerala House, an independent journalist was recording the detention of the AISA president and asking why there was no woman police officer there. She alleges that just then ACP Vivek Bhagat touched her inappropriately. When she objected, the officer left, and a woman constable came to stop her recording.

That evening she went with a fellow journalist to the Parliament Street police station and filed a complaint at around 7.30 pm. According to her colleague, the police did not even mention a medical examination, though the complainant spoke of pain. By Monday morning no FIR had been registered.

The police say the case has been handed to the Crime Branch, which is looking at similar complaints by three more women journalists. Lawyer Vrinda Grover says that not registering an FIR on a molestation complaint against a policeman is itself a crime, and the case should have been registered before any transfer. CPI(M) leader Brinda Karat asked why the victim was being asked for video evidence.

The report quotes another journalist, who said an officer touched her back while she was recording the detention of Yogendra Yadav and Prashant Bhushan, and that her complaint was brushed aside. DIGIPUB and the Press Club of India expressed deep concern over the treatment of women journalists and demanded an FIR, suspension and an independent inquiry.
It is alleged that on Monday the complainant and seventeen others who were demanding an FIR were detained.
nazar: An independent journalist standing on the street has neither a big organisation nor a legal team. When the same police who face the allegation drag their feet over taking the complaint, the message is clear: for women, covering a protest is a double risk.
For both press freedom and women's safety, the law must do its job without delay on such a complaint.
sawal: When the accused is the station's own officer, who will write down justice?
ref: DIGIPUB
An association of digital news outlets that speaks up for independent digital journalism and the rights of journalists.
Cognisable offence
An offence in which the police must register an FIR and start an investigation without the court's permission. Molestation falls in this category.

h: Sugarcane harvest: women in the fields, girls at home, schools empty
dek: After the monsoon, lakhs of families leave Marathwada to cut sugarcane, and women and girls pay the heaviest price for this migration.
body: Every year, as soon as the monsoon ends, lakhs of people from drought-hit Marathwada in Maharashtra set out for the sugarcane fields. The harvest season runs from November to April, and the cane belt stretches from Surat in Gujarat to Belgaum in Karnataka. These workers are called koyta, meaning sickle. The report is from the record-yield season of 2006-07.

The mills hire husband and wife as a pair, a jodi, through a mukadam, or middleman. In the rains they get an advance of a few thousand rupees, which is paid off through the whole season's work. The mukadam keeps a big share of the earnings as commission. Rukmini Shingte, who lives in a hut of cane leaves outside a mill in Ahmednagar, cannot read the slips on which the account of her labour is written.

The pairs leave for the fields at two or three in the night. The camps have neither water nor electricity. Carrying water is the job of women and girls, and there is no cover even for bathing. Girls younger than ten cook for the whole family on cow-dung cakes. Government rations, health services and the anganwadi (village childcare centre) are all left behind in the village.

Sheetal Munde of Beed stayed away from school for six months and then dropped out. Now she cuts cane and sells bundles of leaves for fodder. According to a government survey, about 1.75 lakh (175,000) children were affected by this migration. Many of the sakhar shalas (sugar schools) set up near the mills run only on paper, and girls are the first to be kept back to handle the housework.

The mills are controlled by politicians, who fight for the cane price but not for the rights of the cutters. The employment guarantee scheme did not run at all in many villages, and in one village the sarpanch running the scheme was himself a mukadam.
nazar: This report is many years old, but this week too, bullock carts and trucks are getting ready to leave Marathwada's villages. In later years there were also reports of women cane cutters having their wombs removed. As long as the system of advance debts and hiring in pairs does not change, women will remain workers without wages and girls will stay out of school.
sawal: Who is swallowing the bitterness of sweet sugar?
ref: Koyta and mukadam
A koyta is a pair of cane cutters; the name comes from the sickle. A mukadam is the contractor who gives an advance, takes the workers to the mill and takes a commission.
Sakhar shala
Seasonal schools opened near sugar mills for the children of migrant workers. According to the report, many had no toilet, no water and no benches.

h: A uniform civil code, or the old Hindu law under a new name?
dek: Sadaf Parvez argues that the civil codes of Gujarat and Assam copy Hindu laws, leave out women's real needs and bind live-in relationships with the fear of jail.
body: In September the uniform civil code bills of Gujarat and Assam got the President's assent. After Uttarakhand, three states will now have a single family law for all religions. Sadaf Parvez, who teaches law at Jamia Millia Islamia, says assent makes a law, but it does not prove the model is right.

According to her, these codes stand mostly on the Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 and the Hindu Succession Act of 1956. Because the freedom to make a will remains, parents can write property in their sons' names and cut out their daughters' share. There is no right to shared marital property, the father is preferred in guardianship, and Scheduled Tribes are kept out, while religious minorities are bound.

The practical difficulties are also big. Every divorce will have to go through a court, and a divorce by custom can lead to jail, while crores of cases are already pending in the courts. There is a heavy fine for not registering a marriage, which will hit the poor hardest. Assam's draft was made in just a few days without an expert committee and passed after a few hours of debate.

The most serious question is about live-in relationships. In Gujarat, couples living together for more than a month can be jailed if they do not register a statement, and the information goes to the police and, in some situations, to their families. Citing judgments such as Puttaswamy and Shafin Jahan, the writer says this is an unreasonable attack on privacy, which exposes interfaith, intercaste and queer couples to the very families they want to escape.

She suggests that registration be voluntary and confidential, that abandoned women get firm financial rights, that there be an easy path to divorce by mutual consent, that household labour be counted towards property, and that women's, Adivasi, queer and disability rights groups be truly consulted.
nazar: If a law made in the name of equality lets a daughter's share be taken away by a will, does not count housework as property, and sends the files of couples in love to the police station, it gives women less freedom and more surveillance.
Real reform can come only by talking to women of every community, not by forcing one community's law on everyone.
sawal: How will a law built on surveillance give a woman equality?
ref: Puttaswamy judgment
In 2017, a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held privacy to be a fundamental right under Article 21.
Shafin Jahan case
Known as the Hadiya case, in which the Supreme Court said in 2018 that an adult has the right to choose their own life partner.

h: Stubble smoke now comes more from Madhya Pradesh than Punjab
dek: Satellite data shows that farming's shift towards paddy is changing the map of stubble burning.
body: With the paddy harvest, the stubble-burning season has begun, and this time the leader is not Punjab but Madhya Pradesh. According to the 6 October bulletin of CREAMS, the satellite monitoring group of the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, 287 farm fires were recorded in seven states between 15 September and 6 October.

Of these, 118 were in Madhya Pradesh, 88 in Punjab and 65 in Uttar Pradesh. Rajasthan had 10, Haryana 4, and Delhi and Uttarakhand one each. Of the 33 incidents recorded on 6 October alone, 24 were in Madhya Pradesh. Because of clouds the satellites could not see properly over many areas, which means the real number may be higher.

For Punjab this is the lowest figure for this period in seven years, and so far there has not been a single day with even ten incidents. Haryana also shows a fall. Madhya Pradesh, on the other hand, has its highest figure ever for this period, and fires are rising in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan too.

Looking at the whole of last season, there were 33,028 incidents in six states between 15 September and 30 November, more than half of them, 17,067, in Madhya Pradesh. Uttar Pradesh was second with 7,290 and Punjab third with 5,114.

Experts say Madhya Pradesh is taking the same road Punjab once took. The weather has made soybean, urad and other kharif (monsoon season) crops risky, so farmers are moving to paddy. After the harvest, in the rush to sow the next crop, burning the stubble seems to them the easiest way.
nazar: The stubble debate often gets stuck on Delhi's air and Punjab's farmer. This report shows that the real question is about crop cycles, a changing climate and the farmer's helplessness. These fires will be put out not by fines, but by giving crops like pulses and oilseeds a secure price and insurance, and by taking cheap machines for handling stubble to the villages.
sawal: If the weather pushes the farmer towards paddy, whose fault is it?
ref: CREAMS
A group at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) that uses satellites to monitor farm fires and crops.
Parali (stubble)
The stalks left in the field after paddy is cut. In the rush for the next crop, farmers often burn them, which poisons the air of north India.

h: A new international law for gig workers, and women pushed to the margins again
dek: The ILO's new convention on platform work has a lot in it, but its protection for women who go into homes to work is weak.
body: At the International Labour Conference in June 2026, the ILO passed a new convention, C193, on decent work in the platform economy. The writer, who is linked to WIEGO, a network of workers' organisations, was a representative of the workers' side in this debate. She says the convention gives a minimum floor, but the particular difficulties of women and marginalised people have been largely left out.

Men are the majority in ride and delivery work. Women, and Dalit, minority or queer people, often work in domestic work, beauty services or data work, where they have to go to the customer's home and face the risk of harassment. Yet the convention does not even name sexual harassment. In the debate, 77 percent of the workers' representatives were men, and employers tried to loosen the rules in the name of 'flexibility'.

According to the writer, the United States, Argentina, New Zealand and India put obstacles in the discussion on management by algorithms, yet a clause on it was added. One big win is that whether someone is an employee will now be decided by looking at the reality of the work, not just the label on the contract. But social security and payment for the self-employed have been left to countries.

India's 2020 Code on Social Security does count gig workers, but does not give them rights such as gratuity and PF (provident fund) that employees get, and accepting C193 will not require this to change. According to one report, beauty workers climb stairs in the heat carrying bags heavier than seven kilos, and get bad ratings for asking customers for water. India has also not yet ratified C190, the convention on violence and harassment at work.

The writer concludes that just signing a convention will not change daily life. For that, workers will have to organise, and unions will have to make room in their leadership for women and marginalised people.
nazar: In India, lakhs of women go into other people's homes through apps to clean, cook and do beauty work. The app gives them work and watches them through ratings, but takes no responsibility for their safety. If the government ratifies both C190 and C193 and improves its own laws, it will be a big step for the most vulnerable workers in the unorganised sector.
sawal: If the app gives the work, whose job is it to keep the worker safe?
ref: ILO convention
Member countries of the International Labour Organization together set standards for workers' rights. A country that ratifies a convention has to shape its laws to match it.
The ILO convention of 2019 on protection from violence, sexual harassment and gender-based violence at work. India has not yet ratified it.

h: Srinagar's smart city: shining roads, flooded lanes
dek: On paper Srinagar's smart city project is nearly complete, but one hour of rain showed that the drains, the sewers and Dal Lake are still left to their fate.
body: Srinagar joined the Smart Cities Mission in 2017. In July 2026 the central government told Parliament that 157 of 161 projects were complete and about Rs 3,530 crore had been spent. But on 20 July that same month, just one hour of rain flooded Lal Chowk, Residency Road, Khanyar and even the Secretariat. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah called it shameful and ordered an outside audit.

This long Newslaundry report shows that the money went mostly on beautifying roads, pedestrian markets and fountains, while there was no flood protection project at all. The smart city company says it only relaid the roads and left the old drains underneath as they were. Shopkeepers in Rajouri Kadal say they could see in advance where the water would go, but stayed quiet out of fear. Now they have suffered losses of several lakh rupees.

The city has no separate network of sewers and storm drains at all. Crores of litres of dirty water are pumped from pumping stations straight into the lakes. According to one study, of the 201 million litres of sewage produced each day, about 147 million litres go untreated into the Dal and the Jhelum. The Dal's open water shrank from fifteen to less than thirteen square kilometres between 2007 and 2020. More than eleven lakh (1.1 million) tonnes of waste has piled up at the Achan dump.

No path to accountability is left either. The municipal corporation's term ended in November 2023 and there have been no elections since. The company's board is full of officials. According to an RTI reply, the company does not even know how many jobs the project created.
The report also lists some successes, such as electric buses, which people like.
nazar: If development is decided from above and the city does not even have an elected municipal government, money is spent on things that look good in pictures. Basics like drains, sewers and the lake get left behind, and the price is paid by small shopkeepers, boatmen and children living by the lake.
In Kashmir, where journalists are under pressure and people are afraid to speak, a report like this is in itself a necessary accounting.
sawal: Without a municipal corporation, who was the city made smart for?
ref: Smart Cities Mission

A central government scheme started in 2015, in which a hundred cities were chosen and money was put into roads, traffic, digital infrastructure and urban services. The mission formally ended in March 2025.
Dal Lake
Srinagar's famous lake, the city's identity and the livelihood of thousands of families. Its water keeps shrinking because of sewage, encroachment and silt.

h: The artisans of Kumartuli: a Durga made from Ganga clay
dek: In the potters' quarter of Kolkata, idols are shaped from bamboo, straw and river clay months before the puja, and those who shape them are workers who come from distant villages.
body: Kumartuli in north Kolkata is a centuries-old settlement of potters. Most of the idols that go across the city for Durga Puja are made here, in narrow lanes and sheds of bamboo and tarpaulin. Sinchita Parbat's photo-rich report shows up close the work that nobody notices in the lights of the pandal (festival marquee).

An idol begins with a bamboo frame, called a kathamo. Straw brought from nearby Bagbazar is tied onto it, then smooth clay from the banks of the Ganga is applied, mixed with jute to form different layers. After drying in the sun for three or four days, the fine work is done with brushes and small bamboo tools.

In one workshop, Kartik Pal is bringing out Kartikeya's face in wet clay. The workshop is named after his father. In a shed nearby, Gopal Pal, who has come from Krishnanagar in Nadia district, prepares a special paste used to stick fine cloth onto the idol so that the surface looks like skin.

Most of those who work here are men, and many are from Krishnanagar, called in months before the season. They live in rooms given by the owners. On normal days there is an eight-hour shift, but as the puja comes closer they work through the night, for which they get overtime.

The report reminds us that Kumartuli's first potters also came from Krishnanagar, about three hundred years ago, and settled near the ghat for the river clay. Back then they would live for weeks in the thakurdalan (shrine hall) of zamindars' mansions and make the idols there. On the day of Mahalaya the goddess's eyes are painted, and from there the countdown to the festival begins.
nazar: This season of Navratri and Durga Puja is also a time to remember the hands on whose labour all the splendour rests. Behind the grandeur of the pandal are those same seasonal migrant workers, whose art has come down through generations but whose names are recorded nowhere.
sawal: Who knows the names of the hands that shape the goddess?
ref: Kumartuli
A historic potters' settlement on the banks of the Hooghly in north Kolkata. Durga Puja idols go from here across the country and abroad.
Mahalaya
The day before Durga Puja when Pitru Paksha (the fortnight of the ancestors) ends and Devi Paksha (the fortnight of the goddess) begins. In Bengal the festive mood begins from this day.

h: A confession of killing, and still the file closed: accounting for the Afghan war
dek: Nick Turse's investigation shows that a US soldier confessed to killing an unarmed man in Afghanistan, and the army closed the case in six weeks.
body: In March 2023 a former soldier of the US Army's 82nd Airborne Division walked into a police station in the city of Banning, California, on his own. In front of an officer of the army's investigation department, he admitted that he had killed an unarmed man and wounded a woman, and said he had committed a war crime.

The incident took place in April or May 2010, in the Arghandab valley of Kandahar province. Based on something picked up on the radio, an interpreter said a man on a motorcycle was carrying a rocket launcher. Permission to fire came from above, and about twenty soldiers opened fire. According to eyewitnesses, there was no weapon there. The body was left beyond recognition and a woman was crawling on the ground.

Such was the investigation that no attempt was even made to identify the people killed. The investigators spoke only to soldiers of the same unit, many of whom remembered nothing or said the action was justified. Within six weeks the conclusion was that there was no solid basis for murder, and the file was closed.

Turse does not see this as an isolated case. By the estimate of Brown University's 'Costs of War' project, more than 70,000 Afghan and Pakistani civilians were killed directly in this war. According to one podcast investigation, the army investigated 781 possible war crimes in Afghanistan and Iraq, found no crime in at least 65 percent of them, and the average sentence of those punished was eight months.

A former army lawyer estimates there may have been hundreds of such incidents. The writer links this to the policy of the current defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, under which the safeguards to protect civilians from harm have been loosened.
nazar: People of poor countries who die in the wars of powerful nations often become nameless numbers. When the killer himself confesses and there is still no justice, the question is raised about the whole system.
The price of this war, fought in India's neighbourhood, was paid by ordinary Afghans and Pakistanis. The demand for accountability should be a shared demand of the Global South.
sawal: Who will ask for justice for a death that has no name?
ref: Costs of War
A research project of Brown University in the United States that keeps an account of the human and material losses in US wars since 2001.
Arghandab valley
A fertile valley in Kandahar province in southern Afghanistan, where heavy fighting took place between the US army and the Taliban in 2009-10.

h: Gandhi echoes from Patti Smith to the Brazilian carnival
dek: Tribhuvan's long essay looks for Gandhi's presence in music around the world, and asks what this echo reminds us of today.
body: Published on Gandhi Jayanti, Tribhuvan's essay introduces a Gandhi most Hindi readers do not know. In Western pop, rock, reggae, gospel, folk songs, opera and even rap, Gandhi appears sometimes as a moral touchstone, and sometimes like a rock-star leader of a mass movement.

The writer gives many examples. Patti Smith's 2004 song links Gandhi to Martin Luther King, the American civil rights movement and the time of the Iraq war, and the writer hears in it an echo of the 1930 Salt Satyagraha. Philip Glass's opera Satyagraha rests on the Sanskrit text of the Gita, and its three acts are named after Tagore, Tolstoy and King. In Bahia in Brazil, dock workers formed a carnival group called Filhos de Gandhy in 1949, which carries Afro-Brazilian identity and Gandhi's ideas together.

The essay is not only praise. A study of French songs found 46 songs on Gandhi, and many rappers use him as a joke symbol, the opposite of their tough street image. In some places Gandhi is the face of fashion, in others a mask for anger, and elsewhere an ideal that is impossible to reach.

Tribhuvan also questions India's own songs of remembrance, which are mostly steeped in grief and devotion, and leave out complexities such as Gandhi's political strategy or his differences with Ambedkar.

Drawing on thinkers from Amartya Sen to Hannah Arendt, the writer argues that Indian culture has been many-voiced and built on dialogue, and that non-violence is part of that tradition. In his view, reading Gandhi again through music can be one way of reconnecting with that plurality.
nazar: When at home Gandhi has been turned either into a statue or a target, this essay reminds us that in the wider world, workers, Black citizens and young protesters still see him as a companion in their fight. Non-violence is not something old; it is a living language.
sawal: The world sings Gandhi; how much do we listen to him?
ref: Filhos de Gandhy
A carnival group of Salvador, Bahia, in Brazil, formed by dock workers in 1949. Dressed in white, the group celebrates non-violence and Afro-Brazilian culture together.
Satyagraha (opera)
A 1980 opera by the American composer Philip Glass, based on Gandhi's early struggle in South Africa.
photo_note: Raga Megh Malhar, a Ragamala painting

h: Ram's procession never reached Shabari's hut
dek: Ten poems by Arun Aditya look afresh at the myth of Ram's return in this age of gold, barricades and plunder.
body: This series of ten poems by senior poet Arun Aditya, born in Pratapgarh, reads the story of Ram's return with today's eyes. The editorial note says a return is never as thrilling as a departure; it carries the wounds of the road. Instead of staying locked inside the myth, these poems feel for the hope and grit of ordinary people.

At the heart of the series is Shabari. In one poem she keeps waiting at her hut while the procession passes behind barricades and golden curtains. In another she comforts devotees whose offerings were stolen, and reminds them that the real loss is Ram's own, since he has been locked away out of reach. In a dream Ram tells her that he was always with her, not in some grand temple.

Nishadraj refuses to go and see the grand idol, because so much glitter makes him uneasy. In some poems Ram himself speaks, to Bharat, to Sita, to a remorseful devotee, and says plainly that he cannot be the god of those who take deceit for strength, and that the plundered wealth belongs to the people.

The last poems grow gentle. Ram will return not from the sky but from the same waters of the Saryu where he vanished, and this time he will bring Sita with him, never to leave her again. At Guptar Ghat, an entwined pair of blue and red lotuses makes love the truest form of faith.
The poems hold both satire and tenderness. The target is not religion but the spectacle of religion and the politics that feeds on it. The whole series can be read on Sammukh.
nazar: Taking Ram out of the procession of power and returning him to the huts of Shabari and the Nishad is an old and necessary tradition of Hindi poetry, with roots in both Kabir and Tulsi. These poems say that the first claim on faith belongs to the poor and marginalised people who are kept outside the barricades today.
sawal: Whose home will Ram return to, the palace or the hut?
ref: Shabari
A Bhil woman in the Ramayana who waited for Ram for years and fed him berries she had tasted first. In the bhakti (devotional) tradition she is a symbol of love above caste.
Guptar Ghat
A ghat on the Saryu near Ayodhya where, according to popular belief, Ram took jal samadhi (gave up his life in the water).
photo_note: Ram and Lakshman on a mountain, Shangri Ramayana

h: Laila's death, and the writer's fear
dek: The fourth part of Neha Naruka's prose series links the memory of a girl killed in her in-laws' home to the writer's own fear and silence.
body: This is the fourth part of Mritatmaon ka Desh (The Land of the Dead Souls), a prose series by poet Neha Naruka, who has received the Vagishwari Samman. It is both a story and a confession, and the writer herself admits that what she saw and what she imagined have mixed together in it.

At its centre is Laila, a girl from a small town who is married to a government employee in Delhi. Relatives cannot stop praising the match, but the husband is a coward and the house is ruled by his mother and sisters. One night her drunk brother-in-law makes her grind spices on the grinding stone, and that same night Laila dies. The in-laws call it a hanging; the husband makes up a story of disgrace. Alongside runs the story of the death of another woman, Jyoti.
For years Laila follows the narrator. She even writes a poem about her, but the character refuses to leave; she wants her story to keep being told.

Then the piece turns to the writer's own life: the fear of family, of the state, of colleagues and most of all of the blindly devoted mob, a fear that even makes her ill. Her father pushed her towards biology; writing was a small hobby that could be kept quietly. In the end she sees herself as a woman who has climbed out of the well but still has one foot caught in the deaths of those women.
The tone is broken into fragments, bitter and in places full of satire. The whole part can be read on Sammukh.
nazar: Deaths from dowry and domestic violence are often buried in the single word suicide. Neha Naruka's prose shows that such deaths do not belong to one home alone; they settle as fear inside all the women who escaped. Bearing witness is also the work of literature.
sawal: Who gets away by calling a death in the in-laws' home a suicide?
ref: Vagishwari Samman
A literary award of the Madhya Pradesh Hindi Sahitya Sammelan. Neha Naruka received it in 2024 for her poetry collection.

h: Where a mother's story turns foreign in translation
dek: Through Hindi translations of Korean literature, Rohini Kumari shows how culture and tone slip away as soon as the words change.
body: In this article, published on International Translation Day, Rohini Kumari, who has a PhD in Korean from JNU, examines both the power of translation and its slips. It begins with Han Kang's novel The Vegetarian, which won the 2016 International Booker jointly for the writer and her translator Deborah Smith. Some critics said the English translation strayed from the original, but the writer stood by her translator, and the debate only raised the translator's standing.

Hindi too has seen a flood of translations, not only of novels but also of economics, history and memoirs. Most come by way of English, but some have been done directly from the original language, such as Sonya Surabhi Gupta's translation from Spanish, Ekant ke Sau Varsh (One Hundred Years of Solitude). The writer finds the Hindi translations of Patrick Modiano very literal and awkward.
One interesting observation of hers is that Korean food, dramas and music are very popular in India, yet even good Hindi translations of Korean literature have not reached readers.

A large part of the article is about Shin Kyung-sook's novel Please Look After Mom, which the poet Neelabh rendered into Hindi from English as Maa ka Dhyan Rakhna (Look After Mother). This story of the search for an old mother lost at Seoul Station is very close to the Indian reader, yet in translation the meaning of a verb sometimes goes flat, the exact sense of time sometimes blurs, and the talk between mother and daughter sometimes feels cold and foreign. At each place the writer suggests a more natural Hindi option, not as a final verdict but as a possibility.

The conclusion is balanced: a translation from the original is not automatically better, nor is one done through a bridge language automatically weaker. But access to the original helps to catch relationships, forms of address and cultural cues.
nazar: Hindi mostly sees the world through the window of English. If direct translations from the languages of Asia and the Global South grow, our neighbouring societies will meet us in their own voice, not in a third party's accent. This article is also advice for publishers.
sawal: Through whose language do we read the world?
ref: Han Kang
A South Korean writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2024. The Vegetarian is her most talked-about novel.
Hallyu
The Korean wave: a word used for the worldwide popularity of Korean dramas, K-pop music, food and fashion.

h: Shrikant Verma: a great poet of failure and anger
dek: Ashok Vajpeyi's memoir remembers Shrikant Verma's poetry, his friendship and his politics together, without any whitewashing.
body: Ashok Vajpeyi wrote this memoir years ago, and Janakipul has reprinted it from his collected works on the occasion of his receiving the Shrikant Verma Shikhar Samman. It has both the warmth of friendship and the frankness of a critic.

In Vajpeyi's eyes, Shrikant Verma was a poet of failure and anger, and this anger was aimed more at himself than at society. He compares him to Muktibodh, both of them poets who accused themselves, but Shrikant's inner hell is more personal and offers no easy release. His harsh, at times almost abusive language was chosen with care, and his later poetry makes a restless reckoning with history, myth and death.

The memoir brings the literary world of old Delhi to life: the magazine Kriti, brought out with Naresh Mehta, which put Shamsher and Muktibodh forward against the dominance of Agyeya; the Coffee House at Connaught Place and a meeting there with Lohia; the gatherings of writers and painters. There is mention too of Muktibodh's last illness and his death at AIIMS in 1964, and of how the credit for editing Chand ka Munh Tedha Hai (The Moon's Face Is Crooked) was shared.

Vajpeyi does not look away from Shrikant's politics: his support for the Emergency and his closeness to the Congress are clearly recorded. The controversy over the World Poetry Festival after the Bhopal gas tragedy is also mentioned. But his argument is that weak politics does not cancel the worth of the poetry.
It ends with a last meeting in a New York hospital with Kedarnath Singh, and with the verdict that Shrikant's poetry is among the darkest voices of twentieth-century Hindi.
nazar: Remembering a writer whole, along with his politics, has become hard today, when everyone is made either a god or a villain. This memoir shows that one can record a poet's support for the Emergency and still be honest about his poetry.
sawal: Does a poet's politics decide the verdict on his poetry?
ref: Shrikant Verma
Hindi poet (1931-1986), author of collections such as Magadh and Bhatka Megh (The Lost Cloud). He was linked to the Congress and was also a member of the Rajya Sabha.
Kriti
A literary magazine brought out from Delhi in the late 1950s, started by Shrikant Verma and Naresh Mehta.
photo_note: The End of the Journey, Abanindranath Tagore

h: The artist's courage before an empty canvas
dek: Through Mark Rothko and Pierre Soulages, Kumar Ambuj asks what honesty and freedom cost in art.
body: This long essay by Bhopal poet Kumar Ambuj is not a review of an exhibition but an argument about the relationship between painting and thought. Written in short numbered sections, it makes its case through the lives and words of two painters, Mark Rothko of America and Pierre Soulages of France.

It begins with the artist's struggle before an empty canvas. Ambuj says abstract art too needs thought behind it, and gives the example of Rothko, who waited nearly two decades before putting two colours together on a canvas. In his view, after wars and atrocities, art cannot serve up only decorative flowers and beautiful bodies.

One memorable part of the essay is Rothko's decision to turn down a big commission for a luxurious restaurant in Manhattan, because he could not bear the idea of rich people eating beneath his paintings. According to the writer, the artist has to choose not beauty but the power of creation, and the false courage that comes from intoxication is not enough for this.

The second part is about Soulages, who gave his whole life to the colour black. How light glints in layers of black, and how many colours hide in darkness: Ambuj links this even to cave paintings. There is also the story of Soulages leaving art school, when his teachers warned him that this path would make him enemies.
In the end the essay asks artists to trust their work, because in the end the work outlives both the critics and the market.
nazar: When both the market and those in power ask artists and writers for a convenient silence, this essay reminds us that saying no is also part of creation. For the Hindi reader, finding such serious writing on world art in their own language is no small thing.
sawal: Who does the artist create for, the buyer or the truth?
ref: Mark Rothko
Russian-born American painter (1903-1970), known for abstract paintings of large rectangular blocks of colour.
Pierre Soulages
French painter (1919-2022) who worked all his life on the colour black and the light that glints in it.
photo_note: The Last Unfinished Painting, Amrita Sher-Gil
